item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Emotion-Focused Behavioral Weight Loss Treatment for Adolescents: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Family-based behavioral treatment (FBT) efficacy decreases in adolescence, a developmental period of gradual maturation and increasing autonomy during which emotion regulation skills develop.

Objective: To evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of FBT alone compared with FBT plus emotion regulation across 6 months of treatment and 12 months of follow-up on adolescent weight change, emotion regulation, emotional eating, and parent weight change.

Design, setting, and participants: This parallel-group randomized clinical trial of adolescents 13 to 16 years of age with body mass index (BMI) in the 85th percentile or higher but less than the 99.9th percentile was conducted from August 29, 2019, to January 4, 2024, at 2 university clinics. Central randomization was completed by a statistician, and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment condition. The majority of treatments and assessments were delivered remotely via video conference due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Interventions: FBT plus emotion regulation vs traditional FBT skills alone for weight loss. FBT included nutrition and physical activity education, behavior change strategies, and parenting skills. Both treatments had 6 months of adolescent and parent groups and behavior coaching sessions. The combined group included FBT skills and added dialectical behavior therapy and emotion-focused therapy.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were adolescent weight (body mass index [BMI] z score (BMIz) and BMI as a percentage of the 95th BMI percentile [%BMIp95]), emotion regulation skills (measured by Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale [DERS] scores), emotional eating behaviors (measured by Emotional Eating Scale [EES] scores), parent weight, and feasibility and acceptability of treatment. Primary outcome analyses used an intention-to-treat approach.

Results: A total of 166 (FBT plus emotion regulation = 84; FBT = 82) dyads (adolescents: mean [SD] age, 14.3 [1.2] years; 95 [57%] female; mean [SD] BMIz, 2.2 [0.6]; mean [SD] %BMIp95, 120.4 [21.4]; parents: mean [SD] age, 45.3 [6.5] years; 141 [85%] female; mean [SD] BMI, 32.6 [7.0]) were assessed at baseline, midtreatment, posttreatment, and 6- and 12-month follow-up visits. There were no statistically significant differences in posttreatment weight loss among adolescents receiving FBT plus emotion regulation compared with FBT (difference in BMIz, 0.03 [95% CI, -0.05 to 0.10]). However, adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation did not regain as much weight at the 12-month follow-up (difference in BMIz, -0.09 [95% CI, -0.17 to -0.02]). At the 12-month follow-up, 4% (95% CI, 1%-12%) of adolescents in FBT and 22% (95% CI, 8%-48%) of adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation lost a clinically significant amount of weight (≥0.20 BMIz). At 12 months' follow-up, parent weight (difference in BMI, 0.51 [95% CI, -0.03 to 1.05]) and adolescent emotion regulation (difference in DERS scores, -0.06 [95% CI, -0.25 to 0.50]) did not differ by treatment. By contrast, the FBT plus emotion regulation group had lower scores than the FBT group on emotional eating (difference in EES scores, -0.39 [95% CI, -0.63 to -0.15]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of 166 parent-adolescent dyads, adding emotion regulation skills to FBT did not improve weight loss during treatment but was associated with less weight regain and lower emotional eating through the 12-month follow-up. These findings suggest that adding emotion regulation skills to an FBT program may attenuate weight regain and decrease emotional eating among adolescents.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03674944.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Quantitative Flow Ratio- vs Angiography-Guided Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Secondary Analysis of the FAVOR III China Trial
item.description:
Importance: Whether the association of quantitative flow ratio (QFR)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with long-term outcomes differs according to multivessel disease (MVD) status is uncertain.

Objective: To assess the association of QFR-guided vs angiography-guided PCI with 3-year outcomes according to MVD status.

Design, setting, and participants: In this prespecified secondary analysis of the FAVOR III China randomized clinical trial, patients were screened across 26 centers in China from December 25, 2018, to January 19, 2020. Eligible participants were adults undergoing PCI for stable or unstable angina or for myocardial infarction (MI) occurring at least 72 hours before screening who had at least 1 lesion with 50% to 90% diameter stenosis in a vessel of 2.5 mm or larger. The analysis compared QFR-guided with angiography-guided PCI according to MVD status. MVD was defined by involvement of at least 2 epicardial vessels or the left main coronary artery. The primary analyses of the current prespecified secondary analysis were completed in October 2024.

Interventions: Randomization 1:1 to QFR-guided PCI or angiography-guided PCI.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary end point of the FAVOR III China randomized clinical trial was 1-year major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as a composite of all-cause death, MI, and ischemia-driven revascularization. The current analysis evaluated 3-year MACE.

Results: Among 3825 patients in the intention-to-treat population (mean [SD] age, 62.7 [10.0] years; 2699 [70.6%] male), 2066 (54.0%) had MVD. In the MVD cohort, MACE occurred in 124 of 1023 patients (12.1%) in the QFR-guided group and 188 of 1043 patients (18.1%) in the angiography-guided group (hazard ratio, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.52-0.81; P < .001), driven by lower rates of MI and revascularization. In the non-MVD cohort, MACE occurred in 76 of 890 patients (8.6%) and 95 of 869 patients (11.0%), respectively (hazard ratio, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.57-1.04; P = .09). The treatment × MVD interaction was not statistically significant (P for interaction = .35). The findings of landmark, per-protocol, competing-risk, sensitivity, and hierarchical win-ratio analyses were directionally consistent with the main findings.

Conclusions and relevance: In this prespecified secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial of patients undergoing PCI, QFR-guided PCI was associated with a lower 3-year MACE rate among patients with MVD; however, no significant interaction was observed between treatment effect and MVD status. These findings provide longer-term randomized evidence supporting QFR-guided PCI across MVD strata and warrant further confirmation.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03656848.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Weight Gain During Pregnancy and Severe Maternal Morbidity
item.description:
Importance: Severe maternal morbidity (SMM) carries serious consequences for pregnant individuals, yet the association between gestational weight gain (GWG) and SMM remains poorly understood.

Objective: To examine the association between GWG and SMM across prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) categories.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used linked birth registry data from Better Outcomes Registry & Network Ontario and hospitalization data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information for singleton pregnancies with a hospital delivery at a gestational age of 20 weeks or greater in Ontario, Canada, from April 1, 2012, to March 31, 2022. Data were analyzed from May 1 to November 1, 2025.

Exposures: Continuous GWG as mean weekly gain in the second and third trimesters and categorical GWG (inadequate, adequate, or excessive) according to the 2009 Institute of Medicine recommendations based on prepregnancy BMI.

Main outcomes and measures: SMM, defined as a composite of 13 indicators per the Canadian Perinatal Surveillance System, occurring during delivery hospitalization.

Results: Among 1 035 927 pregnancies, 192 731 (18.6%) had inadequate, 296 448 (28.6%) had adequate, and 546 748 (52.8%) had excessive GWG; 15 119 (14.59 per 1000 births) experienced SMM. Compared with adequate GWG, excessive GWG was associated with increased SMM across all BMI categories: underweight (adjusted rate ratio [ARR], 1.33 [95% CI, 1.15-1.53]), normal weight (ARR, 1.24 [95% CI, 1.17-1.31]), overweight (ARR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.06-1.27]), obesity class I (ARR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.08-1.35]), obesity class II (ARR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.07-1.54]), and obesity class III (ARR, 1.24 [95% CI, 1.03-1.48]). Inadequate GWG was associated with increased SMM predominantly among individuals with normal weight (ARR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.06-1.21]) and overweight (ARR, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.05-1.35]). GWG showed nonlinear associations with SMM across all BMI categories, with risk elevated at both low and high GWG in individuals with underweight, normal weight, and overweight, while in those with obesity classes I to III, risk was concentrated at high GWG values. Estimated SMM rates were lowest at 0.4 kg/wk GWG for underweight through overweight BMI categories and declined across obesity classes to 0.1 kg/wk GWG for the obesity class III category.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 1 035 927 pregnancies, GWG outside Institute of Medicine-recommended ranges was associated with increased SMM risk, with patterns varying by BMI category. These findings may complement existing evidence informing GWG guidance.

Khademioore S, Darling EK, D'Souza R, Muraca GM, Guo Y, Anderson LN

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Telehealth vs In-Clinic Medication Abortion Provision
item.description:
Importance: In states that restrict abortion provision, residents rely on telehealth medication abortion (teleMAB) or travel out of state for in-clinic care; however, little is known about how patients using these modalities differ.

Objective: To compare characteristics of Kansas and Texas residents receiving teleMAB vs in-clinic medication abortion and to assess geographic and socioeconomic factors associated with modality of care.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cross-sectional analysis used electronic medical record data for patients residing in Kansas or Texas who received medication abortion care from a teleMAB service or from an abortion facility in Kansas from February 1 to June 30, 2024. Patients younger than 18 years were excluded because only the telehealth site served this age group.

Exposure: Patient sociodemographic characteristics (age, race and ethnicity, and number of children), gestational age, and county-level distance to the nearest abortion facility, social vulnerability, and rural-urban designation.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was receipt of teleMAB vs in-clinic care. Differences between patients who received teleMAB vs in-clinic care were assessed using χ2 and t tests for bivariate variables and multivariable logistic regression for adjusted comparisons.

Results: The teleMAB service served 12 823 patients (Texas: n = 12 552; Kansas: n = 271); the clinic served 725 patients (Texas: n = 587; Kansas: n = 138). Mean (SD) age was 26 (6) years for Kansas residents and 27 (6) years for Texas residents. In both states, more telehealth patients self-identified as Hispanic, Latino, Latina, or Latine (Texas: 3739 of 12 552 [32%]; Kansas: 48 of 271 [18%]) than in-clinic patients (Texas: 14 of 587 [3%]; Kansas: 8 of 138 [7%]) (P < .001). This difference remained among Texas residents after adjustment. In both states, compared with in-clinic patients, telehealth patients were more likely to be at less than 6 weeks' gestation (Texas: 7648 of 12 552 [61%] vs 155 of 587 [27%]; Kansas: 159 of 271 [59%] vs 45 of 138 [33%]; P < .001) and to have no children (Texas: 5545 of 12 552 [44%] vs 42 of 587 [7%]; Kansas: 137 of 271 [51%] vs 5 of 138 [4%]; P < .001). In Texas, patients who lived farthest from in-clinic care were more likely to receive telehealth than those who lived shorter distances (average marginal effect, 0.003; 95% CI, 0.002-0.004).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of patients who used medication abortion, teleMAB patients more often had no children, were living farther from an abortion facility, and represented populations facing structural racism and long-documented barriers to abortion care compared with in-clinic patients, particularly in abortion-restrictive states. A higher number of patients at lower gestational age received telehealth than in-clinic services, suggesting more convenient and timely care.

item.title: JAMA: Rituximab vs Azathioprine for Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Maintenance Therapy: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: For patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), guidelines recommend considering maintenance therapy after achieving remission. Data comparing maintenance therapeutic options are limited.

Objective: To compare the effects of rituximab and azathioprine maintenance therapies on remission duration for patients with EGPA who recently achieved remission of vasculitis after standard therapy, including prednisone tapering or withdrawal.

Design, setting, and participants: From March 7, 2018, to June 2, 2022, this double-blind, double-dummy, investigator-initiated, superiority, randomized clinical trial enrolled 98 participants with EGPA from 36 hospitals in France. Inclusion eligibility required a new EGPA diagnosis or relapsing EGPA within 30 to 360 days of achieving vasculitis remission (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0 [range, 0-63, with higher scores indicating more severe disease activity]) after a standard induction regimen. Data were analyzed from April 1, 2025, to September 17, 2025. Additional analyses ended June 22, 2026.

Interventions: Participants were randomized to receive a predefined standardized tapering of oral prednisone and either 500 mg of intravenous rituximab every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine placebo for 24 months (n = 49) or rituximab placebo every 6 months for 18 months and daily oral azathioprine for 24 months (n = 49).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary efficacy end point was the duration of total remission during the 28-month study period while taking 7.5 mg/d or less of prednisone. The 14 secondary end points included proportion of participants remaining in remission, rate of vasculitis relapse, and rate of asthma or rhinosinusitis exacerbations.

Results: All 98 randomized participants (mean age, 59.0 years [SD, 14.4]; 50 women [51%]) received at least 1 dose of the trial regimen and 92 (94%) completed the trial. The mean time in remission with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 91.1 weeks (95% CI, 80.9-101.2) vs 96.0 weeks (95% CI, 85.6-106.5) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively (P = .38). The proportion of participants who remained in remission during the 28-month study period with prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less was 17 of 49 (34.7%) vs 11 of 49 (22.4%; relative risk, 1.51; 95% CI, 0.83-2.73; P = .18) in the rituximab and azathioprine groups, respectively. The proportion of participants with at least 1 vasculitis relapse was 7 (14.3%) vs 9 (18.4%) in the rituximab vs azathioprine groups, respectively, and for those with at least 1 clinically significant asthma exacerbation, rhinosinusitis exacerbation, or both, it was 16 (32.7%) vs 19 (38.8%). One participant in the azathioprine group died of SARS-CoV-2 infection before vaccine development. Rituximab recipients experienced a higher incidence of severe infections (23 [46.9%] vs 12 [24.5%], respectively), primarily due to severe SARS-CoV-2 infections.

Conclusions and relevance: For participants with newly diagnosed or relapsing EGPA, rituximab was not superior to azathioprine for improving the duration of total remission during 28 months while taking prednisone at 7.5 mg/d or less.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03164473.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit
item.description:
Purpose: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity.

Methods: A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications.

Results: Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population.

Conclusion: Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

Barletta JF, Erstad BL

item.title: N Engl J Med: Sibeprenlimab in IgA Nephropathy - Final Phase 3 Trial Analysis
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Sibeprenlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, selectively inhibits the cytokine A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), a key driver of IgA nephropathy. Preliminary trial results with regard to the primary end point of the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at 9 months after treatment as compared with baseline have been reported, but secondary end points, including outcomes regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), have not.

Methods: We randomly assigned adults with IgA nephropathy to receive subcutaneous sibeprenlimab (at a dose of 400 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks. The key secondary end point was the annualized slope of the eGFR over 24 months. Other secondary end points included the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months, a composite kidney end point of kidney-function decline or kidney failure, and pharmacodynamic and safety end points.

Results: A total of 510 patients underwent randomization - 259 to receive sibeprenlimab and 251 to receive placebo. The annualized eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area per year (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year (95% CI, -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference, 4.5 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001). The least-squares mean treatment difference for the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months was 9.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, 7.1 to 11.4; P<0.001). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the sibeprenlimab group and in 28 patients (11.2%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -10.8 percentage points; hazard ratio, 0.029; 95% CI, 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 235 patients (90.7%) in the sibeprenlimab group and 226 patients (90.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 21 patients (8.1%) and 32 patients (12.7%), respectively; and serious infections in 5 patients (1.9%) and 10 patients (4.0%). No deaths were reported.

Conclusions: Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline. (Funded by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization; VISIONARY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05248646.).

item.title: N Engl J Med: Atacicept in IgA Nephropathy - Phase 3 Trial Final Efficacy Analysis
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here.

Methods: We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed.

Results: Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m2; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died.

Conclusions: Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).

item.title: Lancet: Endometrial ablation plus levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system versus endometrial ablation alone in women with heavy menstrual bleeding in The Netherlands (MIRA2): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial
item.description:
Background: Endometrial ablation is an established and effective treatment for women with heavy menstrual bleeding, but many patients require further treatment, with approximately 10% ultimately undergoing a hysterectomy within 2 years. The insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) immediately after endometrial ablation might inactivate residual untreated endometrium or prevent its regeneration, thereby preventing recurrent symptoms necessitating a hysterectomy. The aim of the study was to assess whether LNG-IUS insertion immediately after endometrial ablation in women with heavy menstrual bleeding reduced the need for subsequent hysterectomy within 2 years compared with endometrial ablation alone.

Methods: This multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 34 hospitals in the Netherlands. Women younger than 60 years with heavy menstrual bleeding who were eligible for endometrial ablation were included and randomly assigned (1:1) to combined treatment comprising endometrial ablation plus LNG-IUS or to standard care comprising endometrial ablation alone (stratified by dysmenorrhoea and age). Masking was not applied. Endometrial ablation was done using electrical radiofrequency ablation or by transcervical resection of the endometrium. In participants allocated to combined treatment, intrauterine insertion of an LNG-IUS containing a total of 52 mg of levonorgestrel (releasing 20 μg per day in the first year) was done immediately after the ablative procedure. The primary outcome was the incidence of hysterectomy within 2 years, analysed on a modified intention-to-treat basis in all participants with available data. Serious adverse events were systematically assessed at 6 weeks, 12 months, and 24 months after the intervention. This study was registered on the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (NL-OMON54839) and is complete.

Findings: Between Nov 19, 2019, and April 5, 2023, 715 participants were randomly assigned to combined treatment (n=359) or endometrial ablation alone (n=356). The median age of all participants was 45 years (IQR 40-48). 42 (6%) participants had missing data for the primary outcome at 2 years of follow-up. A hysterectomy was done in 15 (4%) of 342 participants in the combined treatment group versus 34 (10%) of 331 participants in the endometrial ablation group, corresponding to a relative risk (RR) of 0·43 (95% CI 0·24 to 0·77; p=0·0050), with a risk difference of -0·06 (95% CI -0·10 to -0·02; p=0·0040). Serious adverse events were reported in 27 (8%) of 346 participants in the combined treatment group and 26 (8%) of 327 participants in the endometrial ablation alone group (RR 0·98, 95% CI 0·59-1·65; p=0·94), and there were no treatment-related deaths.

Interpretation: The combination of endometrial ablation and LNG-IUS significantly reduced the incidence of hysterectomy compared with endometrial ablation alone. The combined treatment appears to be a safe adjunctive strategy for heavy menstrual bleeding that does not increase the risk of complications.

Funding: The Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development.

Oderkerk TJ, Leemans JC, Beelen P, Herman MC, Coppus SFPJ, van der Weide MC

item.title: Lancet: Disease-free survival and overall survival after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer in the Netherlands: results of the single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial
item.description:
Background: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade induces high pathological response rates in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer, yet long-term survival outcomes have not been established. Previously, we reported safety (a primary endpoint) and pathological response (a secondary endpoint) data from the NICHE-2 trial. Here, we report the primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival and the exploratory endpoint of 5-year overall survival.

Methods: In this single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial, patients with previously untreated, clinical stage 2 or 3, resectable dMMR colon cancer received a single dose of intravenous ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) on day 1, and two doses of intravenous nivolumab (3 mg per kg) on days 1 and 15, followed by surgery in one of the six participating hospitals in the Netherlands. Here, we report the independent primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival (time from surgery until disease recurrence or death from any cause) and the secondary endpoint of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) analysis. Overall survival (time from study enrolment until death from any cause) is reported as an exploratory post-hoc analysis. All endpoints were assessed in the per-protocol population (patients who met the eligibility criteria and received at least one cycle of therapy). The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03026140, and has completed accrual.

Findings: From July 4, 2017, to July 18, 2022, 123 patients were screened, of whom 115 were treated and 111 were included in the per-protocol population. At the data cutoff (June 19, 2026), the postoperative median follow-up was 58·7 months (IQR 49·0-72·9). The 3-year disease-free survival was 100% (97·5% CI 100-100). After a median follow-up of 60·4 months (IQR 50·6-74·1), calculated from time of study enrolment, the 5-year overall survival was 100% (95% CI 100-100). In patients with available plasma samples, ctDNA was detected in 99 (92%) of 108 patients at baseline, and ctDNA clearance was observed in 44 (45%) of 98 patients after the first cycle in week 2 and in 80 (82%) of 97 patients after the second cycle before surgery. In patients with a pathological near-complete response and complete response, presurgery ctDNA clearance was observed in 19 (70%) of 27 patients and 60 (92%) of 65 patients, respectively. Assessment for minimal residual disease after surgery revealed that all patients were ctDNA negative.

Interpretation: In patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer, treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery resulted in a 3-year disease-free survival and 5-year overall survival of 100%. These findings support neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a potential standard of care for patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer.

Funding: Bristol Myers Squibb.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Longitudinal pathways from prenatal alcohol exposure and infant behaviors to verbal IQ and working memory
item.description:
Objective: Assess infant behaviors as early predictors of Verbal IQ and Working Memory (V/WM) differences related to prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) from 4 to 21 years of age.

Study design: Longitudinal observational study of 387 infants (60% PAE; 48% male; 81% Black), from birth to 21 years. Verbal IQ or Working Memory was measured at 4, 9, 15, or 21yrs. with tests of intellectual functioning. Infants were administered a visual preference task and the Neurobehavioral Assessment (NB) at birth, the Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence (FTII) at 6.5 /12 mo. and Mental Development Index (MDI) of the Bayley Scales at 6.5, 12, 24 mos. Latent growth curve modeling assessed the association of PAE with V/WM over time, assessing infant behaviors as predictors.

Results: 2-year Bayley MDI (Indirect effect (IE) = -0.11, SE = 0.045; p = 0.015) was linked to both PAE and V/WM. Abnormal NB correlated with V/WM (β = -0.21, p = 0.023; β = 0.23, p = 0.047, for intercept and slope, respectively). FTII at 6.5 months correlated with MDI (β = 0.16, p = 0.007) and FTII at 1 year (β=0.17, p = 0.005). Neonatal visual preference marginally correlated with FTII at 6.5 months (β = -0.13, p = 0.097). All relationships were controlled for other prenatal exposures, the home environment, and blood lead level.

Conclusions: PAE was related to poorer Verbal IQ and WM from 4 to 21 years of age, via 2-year cognitive outcomes associated with 6- and 12-month infant mental and visual recognition performance. Neonatal neurobehavioral abnormalities were related to V/WM independent of PAE. Infant assessments could aid early identification of cognitive sequelae of PAE in high-risk populations.

Singer LT, Schultheis E, Albert JM, Kim JY, Minnes S, Min MO

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Validation of a novel systematic social observation for assessing the social and built environment in neighborhoods surrounding community-based substance use programs
item.description:
Background: Systematic social observation (SSO) quantifies changes in the social and built environment and can be useful for evaluating the neighborhood effects of substance use programs.

Methods: We developed, implemented, and validated an SSO instrument in the Bronx, New York City, and Providence, Rhode Island. Research assistants assessed neighborhoods in the Bronx (4/19/2023-6/22/2023) and Providence (11/4/2024-12/20/2024) following a randomization schedule to minimize temporal biases. We used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and Bayesian multi-level item response theory (IRT) models to derive social and built environment indices and externally validated the measures against arrest data.

Results: EFA for the Bronx (n = 564) and Providence (n = 463) identified three factors assessed with the instrument: drug litter, people, and built environment. IRT-based social and built environment indices exhibited positive spatial autocorrelation (the Bronx Moran's I = 0.393, P < 0.001; Providence Moran's I = 0.068, P < 0.001). In the Bronx, item severity and discrimination were highest for the drug litter factor; item parameters were relatively uniform in Providence. The Bronx index was associated with total (incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 1.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.04-1.95) and drug-related (IRR = 1.60, 95% CI = 1.10-2.32) arrests. The Providence index was not associated with arrests.

Conclusions: Our SSO protocol can be replicated in diverse settings to evaluate the neighborhood effects of substance use programs and broader effects of neighborhood conditions on substance use. The social and built environment indices for the Bronx and Providence may be useful outcomes in future studies. External validation suggests the Bronx index captured drug-related environmental variation; the Providence index may capture variation unrelated to policing patterns.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Association between parental overdose and substance use disorder and youth overdose and SUD: A large linked commercial claims study
item.description:
Background: Youth drug overdoses (OD) and substance use disorders (SUD) are major public health concerns, yet the association between parental and offspring OD is poorly understood and has not been examined using linked insurance claims data. We examined parental OD/SUD associations with youth diagnoses and treatment utilization.

Methods: Using Merative MarketScan (2017-2024), we studied adolescents (12-17) and young adults (18-25) with a first OD or SUD diagnosis linked to parents/guardians (≥6 months enrollment). Participants were classified as Any OD or SUD-only, with OD + SUD as an Any OD subgroup. Exposure was parental OD/SUD history; secondary outcomes were naloxone, medications for opioids use disorder (MOUD), and behavioral health services within 6 months. Logistic regression adjusted for sex and region.

Results: Among 6.5 million youth, Any OD occurred in 0.5% of adolescents and 0.6% of young adults; SUD-only in 0.8% and 2.6%. Parental OD/SUD was associated with higher odds of Any OD and SUD-only in adolescents (adjusted odds ratios [AORs]: 3.6 [95% CI: 3.4 -3.9] and 3.8 [3.5 -3.9]) and young adults (3.7 [3.5 -4.0] and 3.4 [3.3 -3.5]), respectively. AORs for OD + SUD were 4.3 [3.7 -4.9] and 4.1 [3.7 -4.5], respectively. Naloxone and MOUD receipt were descriptively higher among young adults with parental OD/SUD (p < 0.0001); adolescent treatment and behavioral health utilization did not differ meaningfully by parental diagnosis.

Conclusions: Parental OD/SUD history was consistently associated with elevated odds of youth OD and SUD, with modest increases in medication receipt only among young adults. Youth from affected families may benefit from early identification and tailored interventions.

item.title: N Engl J Med: Helicobacter pylori Infection - Advances, Challenges, and the Road Ahead
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
The discovery of Helicobacter pylori has revolutionized the prevention and treatment of gastritis, peptic ulcers, and, most important, gastric cancer. In the past 40 years, enormous progress has been achieved in the clinical and basic research on H. pylori infection. However, challenges in preventing and treating H. pylori infection exist owing to the lack of an H. pylori vaccine and the ever-increasing resistance to antibiotics worldwide. This review summarizes the history of and key milestones in H. pylori research, provides an update on the understanding of the pathogenesis and global burden of H. pylori infection and the screening strategy for the primary prevention of gastric cancer, and focuses on the emerging trends in the management of H. pylori infection.

Li H, Megraud F, Marshall BJ

item.title: N Engl J Med: Ianalumab for the Treatment of Patients with Sjögren's Disease
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Sjögren's disease is a complex, systemic autoimmune disease with no approved targeted therapies. Ianalumab is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody with a dual mechanism of action, depleting B cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and inhibiting B-cell activation and survival through blockade of B-cell activating factor receptor.

Methods: We conducted two 52-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease. Patients in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ianalumab (300 mg monthly) or placebo; patients in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial were assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive 300 mg of ianalumab monthly or every 3 months or placebo. The primary end point was the change from baseline in the score on the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) at week 48 (scores range from 0 to 123, with higher scores indicating greater disease activity). The first key secondary end point in the hierarchical plan for the NEPTUNUS-1 trial was an ESSDAI response (≥5-point reduction) at week 48; for the NEPTUNUS-2 trial, it was the change from baseline in the score on the Sjögren's Syndrome Symptom Diary (SSSD) or EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI) at week 48.

Results: Overall, 275 patients underwent randomization in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial (ianalumab monthly, 137 patients; placebo, 138 patients) and 504 in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial (ianalumab monthly, 168 patients; ianalumab every 3 months, 167 patients; and placebo, 169 patients). In both trials, ianalumab monthly led to a significantly greater decrease in the ESSDAI score at week 48 than placebo, with a between-group difference of -1.3 points (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.6 to 0.0; P = 0.0496) in NEPTUNUS-1 and -1.0 points (95% CI, -2.0 to 0.0; P = 0.04) in NEPTUNUS-2. No significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI scores were observed at week 48. The incidence of serious adverse events was similar with ianalumab and placebo. Nonserious local injection-site and systemic injection-related reactions were more common in the ianalumab groups.

Conclusions: In these two trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease, ianalumab at a dose of 300 mg monthly resulted in a significantly greater decrease in disease activity at week 48 than placebo, although there were no significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI symptom scores. (Funded by Novartis Pharma; NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05350072 and NCT05349214, respectively.).

Mariette X, Grader-Beck T, Finzel S, Schiopu E, Papas A, Devauchelle-Pensec V

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Dual Health and Economic Burden of Multimorbidity in Aging Populations
item.description:
Importance: Population aging is contributing to rising multimorbidity across physical, psychological, and cognitive domains, yet global evidence integrating health and economic burdens in older adults remains limited.

Objectives: To quantify the global health and economic burden of multimorbidity among adults aged 60 years or older and to assess trends from 2000 to 2023.

Design, setting, and participants: This economic evaluation used observational modeling of Global Burden of Disease study 2023 estimates as health inputs and integrated them with macroeconomic, health expenditure, and population data from World Bank Open Data, the World Health Organization Global Health Expenditure Database, and United Nations population data. Health burden analyses covered adults aged 60 years or older in 204 countries and territories from 2000 to 2023, and economic burden analyses covered 180 countries and territories. Data analyses were performed from January 27 to July 22, 2026.

Exposures: Cross-domain multimorbidity spanning physical conditions, psychological disorders, and cognitive disorders, operationalized as 78 multimorbidity combinations.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were years lived with disability (YLDs) per 100 000 population and economic losses. All economic indicators are reported in 2021 international dollars (USD) adjusted for purchasing power parity. Joinpoint regression characterized 2000 to 2023 trends.

Results: From 2000 to 2023, total YLDs increased from 2367.81 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], 1067.67-4969.59) to 2941.68 (95% UI, 1252.99-6816.95) per 100 000 population, while economic losses increased from $80.10 billion (95% UI, $59.60-$104.69 billion) to $363.25 billion (95% UI, $264.04-$502.74 billion). The highest 2023 YLD rate was observed for osteoarthritis and Alzheimer disease and other dementias (369.87 [95% UI, 163.86-752.23] per 100 000 population), whereas the largest 2023 economic loss was observed for osteoarthritis and anxiety disorders ($48.51 billion [95% UI, $31.68-$76.57 billion]). The fastest-growing combination was diabetes, anxiety disorders, and Parkinson disease, with a YLD average annual percentage change (AAPC) of 3.94% (95% CI, 3.79%-4.08%) and an economic loss AAPC of 9.92% (95% CI, 9.69%-10.13%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this economic evaluation of the global health and economic burden of multimorbidity among adults aged 60 years or older, multimorbidity burden increased worldwide, with economic losses growing faster than YLDs. Heterogeneity across sex, country income groups, and disease combinations, together with divergence between disability and economic burden, suggest that policy priorities for aging populations should consider both health burden and economic vulnerability.

Ji W, Zheng J, Guan S, Liu Y, Chen X, Lin Z
Journal Article

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Telemedicine Consultation for Pediatric Trauma in Community ED Visits and Parent Experience of Care: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster-Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Telephone consultations for acutely injured children receiving care in emergency departments (EDs) in nonpediatric trauma centers frequently exclude direct communication and informed decision-making with parents. The use of telemedicine to facilitate real-time expert consultation and parental communication with pediatric trauma specialists is underexplored and may improve family experience and support clinical decision-making.

Objective: To examine the impact of telemedicine on parent experience of care, parent distress, and transfer frequency for acutely injured children presenting to EDs in nonpediatric trauma centers.

Design, setting, and participants: This stepped-wedge cluster-randomized clinical trial recruited patients between November 30, 2020, and November 27, 2022. Participants included families of children younger than 18 years with acute physical trauma presenting to 1 of 10 nonpediatric trauma centers in northern California. Analyses were conducted between June 2023 and March 2026.

Interventions: EDs were randomized to use telemedicine following a standard telephone consultation or the standard of care (telephone consultation only) when consulting with pediatric trauma physicians.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were parent experience of care and parent distress measured 3 days or more following the child's injury. Experience of care was measured using ED Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (CAHPS) questions. Distress was measured using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y survey. Modified intention-to-treat analyses were performed to evaluate outcomes.

Results: The study included 595 children with acute physical trauma with a mean (SD) age of 7.6 (5.1) years, of whom 369 (62.0%) were assigned to telemedicine and 226 (38.0%) to standard of care. Summary scores for parent experience of care 3 days post injury were similar between cohorts (adjusted mean difference [AMD], 0.041 [95% CI, -0.008 to 0.090; P = .10]), as were parent distress summary scores (AMD, -0.031 [95% CI, -0.297 to 0.235; P = .82]). The adjusted odds ratio for transfer of patients assigned to telemedicine was 0.59 (95% CI, 0.16 to 2.16; P = .43). Subscale analyses found significantly higher parental ED discharge and/or transfer experience ratings for patients assigned to telemedicine (AMD, 0.104 [95% CI, 0.023 to 0.186; P = .01]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, telemedicine consultations did not differ statistically significantly from standard care with respect to parent experience of care, distress, and transfer rates. Subscale analyses suggested a potential improvement with telemedicine consultations in parent experience related to ED discharge and interfacility transfers, highlighting a potential benefit in communication and preparation during care transitions.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04469036.

Marcin JP, Rosenthal JL, Tancredi DJ, Rinderknecht T, Hamline MY, Leshikar H

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Fecal Immunochemical Test Outreach for Colorectal Cancer Screening in Community Health Centers: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening is suboptimal among people in traditionally underserved populations, many of whom receive primary care at federally qualified health centers (FQHCs). Mailed fecal immunochemical test (FIT) outreach improves screening, especially in underserved populations, but questions remain about impact over time.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of centralized annual mailed FIT outreach delivered over 3 years to increase CRC screening in FQHCs.

Design, setting, and participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted between June 1, 2021, and May 31, 2024. Sixteen clinics from 2 FQHCs in Southern California were randomly assigned to mailed FIT outreach or usual care for patients aged 50 to 75 years and not up to date with screening.

Intervention: Intervention components followed best practices for mailed FIT outreach and included educational primers, FIT kits, and telephone reminders.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of individuals up to date with any CRC screening after 3 years of intervention (point prevalence); screening at 2 years was a secondary outcome. Due to a resource constraint-related protocol modification, mailed FIT outreach began earlier in year 3, such that some individuals who completed screening in year 2 were not yet due for repeat FIT.

Results: Among 16 clinics serving 20 250 patients, 6 clinics serving 8334 individuals at baseline (4435 aged 55-64 years [53.2%]; 4896 female [58.7%]; 341 Asian [4.1%], 238 Black [2.9%], 2390 Hispanic [28.7%], and 4371 non-Hispanic White [52.4%]) were randomized to intervention and 10 clinics serving 11 916 individuals at baseline (6443 aged 55-64 years [54.1%]; 7250 female [60.8%]; 699 Asian [5.9%], 355 Black [3.0%], 4635 Hispanic [38.9%], and 4436 non-Hispanic White [37.2%]) were randomized to usual care. At year 3, screening was 39.4% (95% CI, 36.3% to 42.6%) in intervention clinics vs 36.5% (95% CI, 31.2% to 42.2%) in usual care clinics, which was not a statistically significant difference (2.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.2 to 9.0 percentage points). At year 2, screening was 37.8% (95% CI, 35.2% to 40.4%) in intervention clinics vs 27.0% (95% CI, 21.8% to 32.9%) in usual care clinics (difference, 10.8 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.9 to 16.7 percentage points).

Conclusions and relevance: This study's findings suggest that centralized mailed FIT outreach could increase CRC screening in FQHCs serving populations with persistent disparities, although maintaining intervention fidelity and providing ongoing implementation support over time are needed for consistent impact.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04941300.

Martinez ME, Roesch S, Largaespada V, Nodora JN, Rabin BA, Castañeda SF

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Denosumab Therapy Duration and Osteonecrosis of the Jaw and Skeletal Events in Bone-Metastatic Prostate Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Denosumab reduces skeletal-related events in bone-metastatic prostate cancer but carries a cumulative risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ). The treatment duration that best balances these risks has not been established in clinical settings.

Objective: To evaluate the association between duration of denosumab treatment and the 3-year cumulative incidence of ONJ and skeletal events.

Design, setting, and participants: This nationwide retrospective cohort study emulated a target trial using Korean Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service data from January 1, 2009, through August 31, 2024; patients were not randomized. A clone-censor-weight approach with inverse probability of censoring weighting estimated 3-year cumulative incidence and risk ratios (RRs), with death as a competing event. Men included in the analysis had bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and initiated oncologic-dose denosumab therapy; men with castration-sensitive disease were excluded.

Exposures: Six strategies defined by 3 durations (≤6, 7-12, and ≥13 months), each as a schedule-flexible group and a schedule-adherent subgroup (intervals ≤12 weeks).

Main outcomes and measures: Three-year cumulative incidence of ONJ and skeletal events (pathologic fracture, spinal cord compression, and surgery to bone) was the primary outcome; a radiotherapy-inclusive conventional composite of skeletal-related events was assessed as a secondary outcome.

Results: Among 3307 men included in the analysis (mean [SD] age, 72.6 [8.6] years; median follow-up, 42.6 [IQR, 26.5-57.4] months), the overall 3-year cumulative incidence was 9.8% (95% CI, 8.7%-11.0%) for ONJ and 4.9% (95% CI, 4.2%-5.7%) for skeletal events. Relative to treatment for 6 months or less, treatment for 7 to 12 months showed a lower risk of skeletal events (3.82% [95% CI, 3.04%-4.80%] vs 5.76% [95% CI, 4.23%-7.79%]; RR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.45-0.97]) and higher risk of ONJ (3.28% [95% CI, 2.41%-4.44%] vs 1.47% [95% CI, 0.86%-2.50%]; RR, 2.22 [95% CI, 1.21-4.11]). Compared with 7 to 12 months, treatment for 13 months or longer was associated with higher risk of ONJ (12.20% [95% CI, 10.86%-13.68%]; risk difference, 8.93 [95% CI, 7.16-10.64] percentage points), without further reduction in risk for skeletal events (3.99% [95% CI, 3.30%-4.82%]; risk difference, 0.17 [95% CI, -1.03 to 1.31] percentage points).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, denosumab treatment for 7 to 12 months was associated with lower risk of skeletal events and a modest increase in ONJ, whereas treatment beyond 12 months was associated with markedly higher ONJ risk but no further reduction of skeletal events. These findings support individualized reassessment of denosumab treatment duration after approximately 1 year.

Kim S, Jung S, Bu S, Kim JW, Pyo SW, Lee GJ

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Initial Enfortumab Vedotin Dose Reduction and Outcomes in Pretreated Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma
item.description:
Importance: Initial enfortumab vedotin (EV) dose selection is increasingly relevant in advanced urothelial carcinoma (UC). Reduced starting doses may be selected for some patients, but their associations with clinical outcomes and tolerability remain uncertain.

Objective: To evaluate the association of physician-selected initial EV dose reduction with clinical outcomes among patients with advanced UC.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective multicenter cohort study of patients with advanced UC who initiated EV monotherapy after platinum-based chemotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibition was conducted at 18 institutions in Korea from January 1, 2023, to May 31, 2025, with follow-up through May 31, 2026. Data were analyzed in June 2026.

Exposures: Initial EV dose reduction at first administration, before treatment-related toxicity. The primary comparison was reduced-dose (≥10% reduction) vs full-dose (<10% reduction) EV monotherapy; post hoc analyses used less than 10%, 10% to 20%, and greater than 20% categories.

Main outcomes and measures: Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were the primary outcomes. Secondary outcomes included objective response and treatment-emergent peripheral neuropathy (PN).

Results: Among 368 patients (median [IQR] age, 68.0 [62.0-74.0] years; 267 male [72.6%] and 101 female [27.4%]), median (IQR) follow-up was 15.4 (8.4-20.0) months. Median PFS was 5.7 months in the reduced-dose group and 6.3 months in the full-dose group (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.24; 95% CI, 0.95-1.61); median OS was 10.1 and 10.5 months, respectively (adjusted HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.81-1.43). Objective response occurred in 65 of 146 response-evaluable patients (44.5%) in the reduced-dose group and 95 of 179 (53.1%) in the full-dose group. Grade 3 or higher PN occurred in 6 of 170 reduced-dose patients (3.5%) and 20 of 198 full-dose patients (10.1%) (adjusted odds ratio, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.09-0.73). In post hoc analyses, reductions exceeding 20% were associated with shorter PFS compared with the full-dose group (adjusted HR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.01-1.95), although the overall 3-group comparison was not statistically significant.

Conclusions and relevance: In this multicenter cohort study, physician-selected initial EV dose reduction was not significantly associated with survival or response outcomes. These findings do not establish equivalence or warrant routine initial dose reduction. The lower incidence of severe PN and the exploratory PFS signal with reductions exceeding 20% are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation.

Kim IH, Kim CG, Jo J, Jung EH, Park JH, Bae WK

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Clinical Outcomes After Recovered, Positive, and Negative Pulse Oximetry Screening Results Among Newborns
item.description:
Importance: Pulse oximetry screening (POS) detects critical congenital heart defects (CCHDs) and other neonatal morbidities, but the clinical significance of initially abnormal results that normalize on repeat testing remains unclear.

Objective: To assess the prevalence and clinical implications of positive, recovered, and negative early POS results in asymptomatic newborns.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study included asymptomatic neonates born at 35 weeks' gestation or later who underwent early POS at 2 to 6 hours of age at a tertiary-level university hospital in Eastern Finland between January 1, 2012, and December 31, 2019. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to August 2026.

Exposure: Positive POS result or indeterminate POS result that normalized to a negative POS result (recovered) with repeat testing.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission and continued hospitalization at 7 days; secondary outcomes included diagnostic investigations and neonatal morbidities. Associations between POS screening results and outcomes were examined using modified Poisson regression adjusted for maternal age, parity, body mass index, and cigarette smoking during pregnancy and newborn sex, gestational age, and birth weight Z score.

Results: The cohort included 16 599 newborns born at 35 weeks' gestation or later who underwent early POS at 2 to 6 hours of age (8349 [50.3%] female; mean [SD] gestational age, 39.8 [1.3] weeks). POS results were negative in 16 160 newborns (97.4%), recovered in 208 (1.3%), and positive in 231 (1.4%). Compared with a negative POS result, a recovered or positive POS result was associated with higher risk of NICU admission (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 5.62 [95% CI, 4.58-6.91] and 13.04 [95% CI, 11.77-14.44], respectively) and continued hospitalization at 7 days (ARR, 4.70 [95% CI, 3.07-7.19] and 11.97 [95% CI, 9.26-15.47], respectively). Recovered POS was also associated with greater risk of antibiotic exposure before 72 hours of life (ARR, 5.45 [95% CI, 3.94-7.52]) and need for respiratory support (ARR, 10.16 [3.53-29.21]) compared with a negative result. Respiratory disease was more common in newborns with recovered than negative POS results (27 [13.0%] vs 214 [1.3%]), as were sepsis (10 [4.8%] vs 127 [0.8%]) and hypoglycemia (17 [8.2%] vs 565 [3.5%]). No CCHD occurred among newborns with recovered POS.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of neonates born at 35 weeks' gestation or later, those with initially indeterminate POS results that normalized on repeat testing had increased risks of treatable neonatal conditions and hospital care but not of CCHD. Further prospective studies should investigate whether targeted assessment of these newborns could reduce morbidity and prolonged hospitalization.

Karppi L, Kiviranta P, Sankilampi U

item.title: JAMA: Childhood Cancer Risk After Assisted Reproductive Technology
item.description:
Importance: Childhood cancer risk after assisted reproductive technology (ART) remains uncertain, particularly by procedure and cancer type.

Objective: To examine associations between ART and childhood cancer overall and by ART modality and cancer type.

Design, setting, and population: Nationwide Danish cohort of 1 086 136 live-born children from 1996 to 2012, of whom 37 228 (3.4%) were conceived using ART, with follow-up through 2023.

Exposures: Maternal ART, classified as in vitro fertilization (IVF), intracytoplasmic sperm injection, or frozen embryo transfer.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident childhood cancer. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs); Poisson models estimated incidence rates. Non-ART births were the primary reference; secondary analyses used children of women with a history of infertility and children conceived using IVF as reference groups.

Results: During a median follow-up of 20 years, 3736 cancers occurred. Compared with non-ART births (incidence rate, 18.3 per 100 000 person-years), children conceived using ART had higher cancer incidence (incidence rate, 23.6 per 100 000; HR, 1.26 [95% CI, 1.07-1.48]). Rates were higher after frozen embryo transfer (incidence rate, 41.1 per 100 000; HR, 2.18 [95% CI, 1.45-3.29]) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (incidence rate, 27.9 per 100 000; HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.16-1.89]) but not IVF (incidence rate, 18.5 per 100 000; HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.79-1.28]). Frozen embryo transfer was associated with leukemia (incidence rate, 11.1 per 100 000; HR, 2.36 [95% CI, 1.06-5.28]), lymphomas (HR, 3.03 [95% CI, 1.13-8.12]), and soft tissue sarcomas (HR, 7.63 [95% CI, 2.82-20.62]); intracytoplasmic sperm injection was associated with lymphomas (incidence rate, 4.6 per 100 000; HR, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.07-3.54]), soft tissue sarcomas (incidence rate, 3.3 per 100 000; HR, 3.28 [95% CI, 1.54-7.00]), and central nervous system neoplasms (incidence rate, 8.2 per 100 000; HR, 1.63 [95% CI, 1.04-2.57]); no associations were observed for IVF. Findings were similar in secondary analyses using children of women with a history of infertility and children conceived using IVF as reference groups.

Conclusions and relevance: ART, particularly frozen embryo transfer and intracytoplasmic sperm injection, was associated with increased childhood cancer risk, but absolute risks were low. The consistent results in secondary analyses of children with maternal infertility history or conceived via IVF suggest that procedure-related, rather than infertility-related, factors warrant further investigation.

Mose K, Kjaer SK, Jensen A, Grell K, Pottegård A, Hargreave M

item.title: JAMA: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years: A Review
item.description:
Importance: Obesity affects 15% of children aged 2 to 5 years and 22% of children aged 6 to 11 years in the US. Obesity in children is associated with dyslipidemia, hypertension, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnea. Compared with normal-weight peers, children with obesity have lower quality of life and are 5 times more likely to have obesity in adulthood.

Observations: Body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) is used to identify children at risk for excess adiposity, and guidelines recommend that clinicians screen for obesity using BMI starting at age 2 years. Among children, obesity is defined using standardized age- and sex-specific growth charts, with obesity defined as BMI in the 95th or higher percentile and severe obesity as BMI of 120% or greater of the 95th percentile. Obesity treatment in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, consisting of at least 26 contact hours of face-to-face group or family-based activities that incorporate nutrition, physical activity, and behavior change education delivered to the child and caregivers over a 3- to 12-month period. Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment reduces BMI by 0.7 compared with children who do not participate in intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment. The only obesity pharmacotherapy currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for children younger than 12 years is setmelanotide, a melanocortin-4 receptor agonist, which is indicated for 3 forms of rare monogenic obesity (LEPR, POMC, and PCSK1 genetic variants), Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and acquired hypothalamic obesity. Liraglutide is currently only FDA approved for youth aged 12 years or older; however, a randomized clinical trial among children aged 6 to younger than 12 years demonstrated that, compared with placebo, liraglutide reduced BMI by 7.4%. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is rarely used in children younger than age 12 years and evidence supporting its use in children is limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.

Conclusions and relevance: Obesity in children is associated with chronic disease, such as hypertension, and with poor quality of life. Evidence-based treatment for obesity in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, and pharmacotherapy may provide additional benefit, although short- and long-term safety and efficacy data are limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.

Fox CK, Armstrong SC, Kelly AS

item.title: Crit Care Med: Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
item.description:
Objectives: We aimed to assess trends in septic shock publications by country income and author gender.

Data sources: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for articles indexed with "septic shock" between January 2014 and December 2024.

Study selection: All peer-reviewed publication types were eligible. Conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed material were excluded.

Data extraction: Bibliographic data, first and last author affiliations, country income level (World Bank classification: low- and middle-income countries [LMICs] and high-income countries [HICs]), and journal prestige (SCImago Journal Rank [SJR]) were extracted. Author gender was inferred using the NamSor application programming interface (API).

Data synthesis: Of 10,352 eligible publications, LMIC-affiliated first authors increased over time (+2.13% per year; 95% CI, +1.66 to +2.61; p < 0.001) from 18% in 2014 to 37% in 2024. Women represented 35.6% of first authors and 25.0% of last authors (with around 20% of authors not classifiable by the NamSor API), with higher proportions in LMICs than HICs (p < 0.001) for both first authors (44.5% vs. 32.5%) and last authors (35.2% vs. 21.5%). Gender concordance was more frequent, with female first authors more often paired with female last authors than male first authors (31.7% vs. 21.1%). Cross-income collaborations, especially involving LMIC last authors, remained rare. Articles led by men in HICs were more often published in higher-SJR journals compared with those led by women (p < 0.001), whereas no gender differences were observed among LMIC-affiliated authors.

Conclusions: Despite encouraging growth in LMIC contributions and female representation, major inequities persist. Strengthening equitable collaborations and supporting underrepresented groups would broaden participation and enhance the global applicability in critical care research.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
item.description:
Objectives: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings.

Data sources: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase.

Data selection: We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT.

Data extraction: Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes.

Data synthesis: Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012).

Conclusions: A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Furosemide Stress Test in Adults and Children With Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic utility of the furosemide stress test (FST) for acute kidney injury (AKI) management in critically ill adults and children.

Data sources: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to March 3, 2026.

Study selection: Studies evaluating the standardized FST protocol in critically ill adults or children with AKI were eligible. Outcomes included AKI stage 3 progression (Q1), kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation (Q2), short-term mortality (Q3), successful KRT liberation (Q4), and FST-guided vs. standard KRT initiation in randomized trials (Q5).

Data extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 and Risk of Bias 2. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

Data synthesis: Twenty studies (n = 1979; 11 countries; 2013-2025) were included. For AKI progression (nine studies; n = 501), pooled sensitivity was 0.69 and specificity was 0.88 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.89; GRADE: low). For KRT initiation (nine studies; n = 952), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.75 (AUC, 0.79; GRADE: very low). For mortality (six studies; n = 487), sensitivity was 0.56 and specificity was 0.76 (AUC, 0.75; GRADE: very low). For KRT liberation (three studies; n = 177), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.87 (AUC, 0.89; GRADE: low for sensitivity, very low for specificity). The effect of FST-guided early KRT initiation on short-term mortality was uncertain (pooled risk ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.79-1.27; two randomized controlled trials, n = 212; GRADE: very low). Pediatric analyses yielded AUC values of 0.81 and 0.63 for KRT initiation and mortality, respectively.

Conclusions: Based on low to very low certainty evidence, the FST may support risk stratification for AKI progression and KRT liberation in critically ill adults. Its impact on mortality when guiding early KRT initiation remains uncertain. As a low-cost bedside test, the FST can be a useful tool in resource-limited settings where novel biomarkers are inaccessible.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Pediatric Clinical Interventions and Adverse Safety Events Among Emergency Medical Services Encounters in Agencies With and Without a Pediatric Emergency Care Coordinator: An Observational Study
item.description:
Objectives: The purpose of this study was to compare the frequency and types of adverse safety events (ASEs) and potential harm in a diverse population of pediatric emergency medical services (EMS) encounters. As a secondary aim we evaluated the association between prehospital pediatric emergency care coordinators (PECCs) in EMS agencies on the frequency, type and harm severity of ASEs.

Methods: This was a cross-sectional study of EMS and hospital records for children <18 years who received care from 15 EMS agencies from 2019 to 2023, using a validated ASE chart review tool. Frequency and types of ASEs associated with three different categories of clinical interventions (procedures, medication, and fluid administration) were captured. ASEs were assigned to three severities of harm: Harm Unlikely, Mild Temporary Harm, or Permanent/Severe Harm. EMS Physicians verified ASEs and harm severity.

Results: There were 2219 records included in the analysis, 995 from PECC agencies (44.8%). Median patient age was 12.5 years (IQR 6-15). In total, 551 (55.4%; CI: 52.3, 58.5) PECC agency patients had a procedure compared to 328 patients of agencies without a PECC (26.8%; CI: 24.3, 29.3; p < 0.001). Compared to non-PECC agency patients, PECC agency patients were more likely to receive medications (23.4% vs 7.7%, p< 0.001) and receive intravenous fluids (12.9% vs 4.6%, p< 0.001). In total, 290 ASEs were identified, the most frequent of which was the failure to perform a procedure or administer a medication or fluids (43.1%, CI: 37.4, 48.8). There were differences between PECC and non-PECC agencies in the frequency of ASEs in procedures (13.7% vs, 20.0%, p = 0.003). The assigned severity of ASE Mild Temporary and Permanent/Severe Harm was lower for procedures in PECC versus non-PECC agencies, respectively (28.6%, CI: 29.5, 48.5 and 63.3%, 95% CI: 69.6, 88.4, p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Compared to non-PECC agency care, pediatric care by PECC agencies was associated with more procedures, medication and fluid administration, but fewer ASEs for procedures and lower severity of harm when an ASE occurred. These results indicate that the PECC role may be associated with increased interventions and a reduction in harm associated with procedural care.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Delay From Hypotension Onset to Appropriate Antifungal Therapy Initiation Is the Critical Determinant of Outcome in Candida Septic Shock
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the effect of delays in initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy from the initial onset of persistent hypotension to the outcome of Candida septic shock.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: A total of 32 academic and community hospitals in Canada, the United States, and Saudi Arabia (July 1989 to June 2018).

Patients: A total of 850 adult patients with culture-positive Candida septic shock.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Out of 850 patients with Candida septic shock, 69.2% patients (589) received appropriate antifungal therapy after the onset of persistent hypotension. A strong relationship was observed between the delay in initiation of pathogen-appropriate antifungal (PAA) therapy and hospital survival. The adjusted odds ratio of death was 1.045 per hour of delay (95% CI, 1.035-1.056; p < 0.0001). The survival rate was 86% when an appropriate antifungal for the isolated pathogen was administered within 2 hours of the initial documentation of persistent hypotension. Thereafter, hospital survival decreased an average of 5.0% per hour for each hour of delay to 10-12 hours of delay. In a multivariate analysis, which included the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score and epidemiologic/therapeutic variables, the time to initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy emerged as the single strongest predictor of outcome. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that the adverse effects of delayed antifungal treatment were consistent across various subgroups, including different types of infections, pathogens, and antifungal drug classes. Median time to appropriate antifungal therapy was 32.3 hours (interquartile range, 11.2-66.0 hr), with only 16.9% receiving therapy within 6 hours of hypotension onset.

Conclusions: Administration of PAAs within the first hours of documented hypotension significantly improved hospital survival. Less than 20% of patients received appropriate antifungals within 6 hours of documented hypotension.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial
item.description:
Objectives: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach.

Design: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally.

Setting and patients: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours.

Interventions: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation.

Measurements and main results: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy.

Conclusions: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.
