item.title: Chest: Effect of clarithromycin on the circulating inflammatory proteome in community-acquired pneumonia: a secondary analysis of the ACCESS trial
item.description:
Background: The ACCESS randomized double-blind controlled trial in hospitalized adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) showed that adding clarithromycin to standard-of-care therapy accelerated clinical recovery within the first 72 hours after the commencement of treatment and reduced progression to organ dysfunction.

Research question: Does clarithromycin treatment modulate the circulating inflammatory protein profile in CAP, and can inflammatory endotypes identify patient subgroups with distinct clinical responses?

Study design and methods: Serum samples obtained from ACCESS trial patients at baseline and 72 hours were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint. After quality control, 70 proteins from 394 paired samples across 197 patients were analyzed to assess differential expression within and between groups over time, evaluate associations with clinical outcomes, and identify immune endotypes using unsupervised clustering.

Results: IL6 was selectively downregulated on day 4 in the clarithromycin arm, whereas IFN-γ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and SCF decreased over time across both treatment arms, consistent with resolution of inflammation. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. Clustering consistently identified two inflammatory endotypes with comparable SOFA, but distinct RSS scores. The endotype with lower RSS demonstrated higher IFN-γ and globally elevated inflammatory protein expression; in that endotype 90-day mortality was decreased with clarithromycin treatment.

Interpretation: Clarithromycin exerts measurable immunomodulatory effects in CAP, characterized by attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL6. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies.

Clinical trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724044, EudraCT 2020-004452-15.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Massive Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in an Adolescent Patient: A Case Report
item.description:
Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in pediatric patients arises from diverse etiologies that vary across age groups. Although it is an uncommon cause of life-threatening hemorrhagic shock, prompt recognition and management are essential. Owing to the infrequency of hemorrhagic shock from GI bleeding in pediatrics, emergency physicians may lack familiarity with its diagnosis and management. Furthermore, multiple etiologies may coexist and may not be detected during the initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy, increasing the risk of premature diagnostic closure.

Case report: A 17-year-old boy with a history of plaque psoriasis was transported by ambulance to the pediatric emergency department of an urban level one trauma center, presenting with copious hematemesis and hemodynamic instability. Initial resuscitation in the emergency department included blood transfusion, followed by admission to the pediatric intensive care unit. The first endoscopic evaluation by pediatric gastroenterology identified duodenal erosion; however, the patient experienced further large-volume bleeding out of proportion to these findings. A subsequent endoscopy revealed a Dieulafoy lesion, which was treated successfully. The patient was ultimately discharged home and has remained stable during long-term follow-up. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: Although severe GI bleeding in pediatric patients is uncommon, emergency physicians must quickly identify hemorrhagic shock across all age groups and be familiar with the broad differential diagnoses that vary by age. Initial management must prioritize airway protection and hemodynamic stabilization as a bridge to definitive intervention. Clinicians should recognize the limitations of endoscopic gastroduodenoscopy and consider the potential for concurrent sources of bleeding that may necessitate additional intervention. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. item.title: J Emerg Med: Birthday Blues: Clinical Patterns of Emergency Department Visits Surrounding Birthdays
item.description:
Background: Smaller studies have suggested that patients are more likely to present to the emergency department around the time of their birthdays. However, no multi-year analysis has been performed within the U.S. to uncover a possible association between birthdays and presentation to the emergency department (ED).

Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the overall frequency year after year of visits to the Emergency Department and the medical conditions most frequently encountered around the time of a birthday.

Methods: We studied emergency department visits from May 2018 to May 2024 at a Level 1 Trauma Center in a metropolitan city in the U.S.. Our analysis assessed the interval before or after ED presentation with respect to a patient's birthday. We utilized timeframes of ± 7 days (7 d) of one's birthday, ± 14 days (14 d), and ± 30 days (30 d) for analysis. We then conducted a descriptive analysis comparing proportions, standardized ratios (SR), and obtaining predictive probabilities from a multivariate logistic regression model.

Results: Of the 310,047 unique ED visits from 2018 to 2024, 12,650 visits were within ±7d of a patient's birthday. There were a greater than expected number of presentations ±7 d for all genders and age groups (particularly those <18 years old), and for those identifying as Asians. When looking at the role of chief complaint, individuals with a chief complaint related to Psychiatric/Toxicology, Trauma, Dermatologic, and Musculoskeletal concerns had a higher incidence of ED presentation ±7 d.

Conclusion: Across all populations, birthdays appear to be associated with an elevated risk of serious illness.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Age and intensive care unit admissions following opioid overdose
item.description:
Background: Older adults are increasingly impacted by the opioid crisis, yet age-related differences in overdose presentation, management, and outcomes leading to intensive care unit (ICU) admission remain poorly characterized. This study examined age-related variations in drug exposures, interventions provided, and hospital utilization among patients experiencing an opioid overdose.

Methods: The Toxicology Investigators Consortium (ToxIC) Fentalog Study was conducted at 10 US medical centers and collected data on patients who presented to emergency departments with confirmed non-fatal opioid overdose, and available waste serum samples between 9/21/2020-4/14/2026 were included. Chart reviews captured presentations, treatments, and hospital utilization. Toxicologic analyses were performed at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education. Nested multivariable logistic regressions assessed whether age improved predicted ICU admission, after accounting for sociodemographic characteristics and drug classes detected.

Results: Among 1930 patients, 15.3% were admitted to the ICU, 7.8% received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and 5.8% were intubated. Length of hospital stay varied by age, with patients 65 + years old staying longest (median: 22.0h, IQR: 87.0, p < 0.001). Illicit opioids were less commonly detected in older adults (p < 0.001), while prescription opioids were more common (p < 0.001). Age cohort did not significantly predict ICU admission, although prescription benzodiazepine (AOR: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.1, 1.9) and opioid (AOR: 0.7, 95% CI: 0.5, 0.9) detection did.

Conclusions: Older age was associated with longer hospital stays but did not predict ICU admission after adjustment for relevant covariates. Benzodiazepine and opioid exposures showed a modest association with ICU utilization. Further work should clarify how pharmacologic combinations influence clinical severity across age groups.

item.title: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open: Emergency Medical Technician Program Certification Pass Rates by Size and Geographic Region: A Five-Year Descriptive Analysis
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Objectives: Emergency medical technician (EMT) educational programs demonstrate student certification performance variability. Prior evaluations identified program size and regional disparities, yet whether these patterns persist is unclear. This study described national variation in EMT certification pass rates by cohort size, geographic region and cohort year.

Methods: We conducted a repeated cross-sectional descriptive analysis of United States civilian EMT annual program cohorts from 2018 to 2022 using National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians Cognitive Examination data. We included cohorts with >5 candidates testing annually. Cohorts were grouped by fixed cohort size quartiles (Q) and National Association of State EMS Officials (NASEMSO) region. Outcomes were first- and cumulative third-attempt pass rates. Descriptive statistics summarized cohort characteristics and outcomes, and pairwise comparisons assessed group differences.

Results: Of 10,923 EMT educational program cohorts identified, 8567 (78.4%) were included. Median first- and cumulative-third attempt pass rates were 63.9% (interquartile rate [IQR]: 50.0, 77.7) and 77.8% (66.7, 88.3), respectively. Pass rates varied by cohort year, cohort size, and region. Median pass rates were highest in 2022. Q4 (≥46 candidates) had higher median first-attempt and third-attempt rates compared with Q1 (6-10) (first: 68.2%, 60.0%; third attempt: 81.6%, 71.4%). West NASEMSO region cohorts had higher median pass rates than all other regions.

Conclusion: From 2018 to 2022, EMT program success varied across cohort size, geographic region, and cohort year. Larger cohorts had higher median pass rates, and NASEMSO West cohorts had the highest median pass rates. These findings support continued EMT program evaluation and highlight the need for more education data to understand mechanisms for differences.

Kamholz JC, van den Bergh SL, Gage CB, Riel KM, Powell JR, Panchal AR
